1.title: CDMP FUNDAMENTALS
1.text: Welcome to Module 4: Data Architecture. This is Chapter 4 of the DMBOK, worth about six percent of the exam — roughly six questions. Data Architecture is where business strategy meets technical design. In this module you'll learn how organizations create the master blueprints that align their data with their business goals, and you'll meet the famous Zachman Framework, which the exam genuinely loves to test. Let's get into it.

1.title: Module Overview & Learning Objectives
1.text: Here's our plan. You'll learn the definition of Data Architecture and its three goals. You'll name the four Enterprise Architecture domains and see how they depend on each other. You'll work through the Zachman Framework — its six-by-six matrix, the columns, and the rows. You'll understand the Enterprise Data Model and its four levels of abstraction, plus the idea of data flow design. You'll learn the three-to-five-year roadmap. And you'll be ready for questions on implementation risks, cultural factors, and metrics. Let's begin with the definition.

1.title: What Is Data Architecture?
1.text: The DMBOK defines Data Architecture as identifying the data needs of the enterprise — regardless of structure — and designing and maintaining the master blueprints to meet those needs. Those master blueprints then guide data integration, control the data assets, and align data investments with business strategy. There's also a formal ISO definition worth knowing: architecture is the fundamental organization of a system — its components, their relationships, and the principles governing its design and evolution. And note that the word "architecture" is overloaded: it can refer to the current state, the future state, the discipline itself, the artifacts, or even the team. But the phrase to anchor on is master blueprints. Data Architecture is the bridge between business strategy and technology execution — keep that image in mind throughout this module.

1.title: The 3 Goals of Data Architecture
1.text: Data Architecture has three goals. First, identify the data storage and processing requirements — what data needs to be kept and worked on. Second, design the structures and plans to meet both the current and the long-term data requirements of the enterprise. And third — this one is about agility — strategically prepare the organization to quickly evolve its products, services, and data so it can seize opportunities in emerging technologies. That third goal is the forward-looking one: architecture isn't just about today's needs, it's about positioning the organization to move fast tomorrow.

1.title: Business Drivers — The 5 Roles of a Data Architect
1.text: So what does a data architect actually do? The DMBOK describes five roles, and together they show that the architect is far more than someone who draws diagrams. First, they strategically prepare the organization for emerging technologies. Second, they translate business needs into data and system requirements, so business processes consistently get the data they need. Third, they manage complex data and information delivery across the whole enterprise. Fourth, they facilitate alignment between the business and IT. And fifth, they act as agents for change, transformation, and agility. Notice that recurring theme — the architect is a translator between business and IT, and a change agent. That framing often shows up in exam answers.

1.title: The 4 Enterprise Architecture Domains
1.text: Data Architecture doesn't exist in isolation. It's one of four Enterprise Architecture domains, and you should know all four. Business Architecture covers how the enterprise creates value — its models, processes, capabilities, and vocabulary. Data Architecture covers how data is organized and managed — data models, definitions, mappings, and flows. Applications Architecture covers the structure and function of applications — the business systems, software, and databases. And Technology Architecture covers the physical technology that enables everything to run — platforms, networks, security, and integration tools. The key exam point is simply that Data Architecture is one of four EA domains; it works alongside the other three, not on its own.

1.title: The EA Dependency Chain
1.text: These four domains aren't just a list — they depend on each other in a logical chain, the stack you see on screen, and understanding that chain helps you reason about exam questions. Business Architecture comes first; it establishes the requirements. Data Architecture then manages the data that the business creates and requires. Application Architecture acts on that data according to the business requirements. And finally, Technology Architecture hosts and executes the applications. So the flow runs: business sets the requirements, data supports them, applications act on the data, and technology hosts the whole stack. Business, then Data, then Applications, then Technology.

1.title: Enterprise Architecture Frameworks
1.text: To organize all of this, we use enterprise architecture frameworks. A framework is a foundational structure for developing a broad range of related architectures — you can think of it as an architecture for architecture. The relevant standard is ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010, the architecture description standard. The major frameworks you might encounter are Zachman, which we'll dig into next; TOGAF, with its Architecture Development Method; FEAF, the US federal framework, which includes a Data Reference Model; and DoDAF, from the Department of Defense. One exam-relevant detail: in TOGAF's ADM, Phase C — Information Systems Architecture — is the phase that covers data and application architecture. But the framework the CDMP exam focuses on most is Zachman.

1.title: The Zachman Framework — Overview
1.text: The Zachman Framework was developed by John Zachman in the 1980s, and it's the most well-known enterprise architecture framework in existence. Here's what you must understand about it. First, it's an ontology — the six-by-six matrix on screen — that represents the complete set of models needed to describe an enterprise and the relationships between them. Second, and this is the single most tested point: Zachman defines what models should exist — it does not tell you how to create them. It's a classification scheme, not a methodology. Third, each cell of the matrix represents a unique type of design artifact, formed by the intersection of a row and a column. So whenever you see a Zachman question, anchor on this: it shows what, not how. If an answer claims Zachman prescribes a method or a how-to, it's wrong.

1.title: Zachman — The 6 Columns (Interrogatives)
1.text: Let's look at the columns. The six columns of the Zachman matrix are the communication interrogatives — the basic questions you can ask about anything. What, which is the inventory column — the entities or things. How, the process column — the activities performed. Where, the distribution column — business and technology locations. Who, the responsibility column — roles and organizations. When, the timing column — events, cycles, and schedules. And Why, the motivation column — goals, strategies, and means. An easy way to remember them: they're just the classic questions — what, how, where, who, when, and why. Six interrogatives, six columns.

1.title: Zachman — The 6 Rows (Perspectives)
1.text: Now the rows, which represent different stakeholder perspectives, moving from the most abstract at the top to the most concrete at the bottom. Row one is the Executive, acting as Planner — defining scope and context. Row two is Business Management, the Owner — business concepts. Row three is the Architect, the Designer — the system logic. Row four is the Engineer, the Builder — the technology physics. Row five is the Technician, the Implementer — component assemblies. And row six is the User, the Participant — the operational, running instances. Here's the detail the exam likes: row six, the User or Participant level, has no models — it's the actual functioning enterprise, not a representation of it. The rows are called reification transformations, which just means translating an abstract idea, step by step, into a concrete instance.

1.title: Enterprise Data Architecture = EDM + Data Flows
1.text: Let's narrow from enterprise architecture down to Enterprise Data Architecture specifically. Enterprise Data Architecture defines the standard terms and designs for the elements that matter to the organization, describing how data is collected, stored, integrated, moved, and distributed. And here's a key exam fact: Enterprise Data Architecture must include two distinct outputs. The first is the Enterprise Data Model — the holistic structure of the data. The second is the Data Flow Design — how that data actually moves across data stores, applications, platforms, and networks. So whenever you think Enterprise Data Architecture, think two halves: the Enterprise Data Model plus the Data Flow Design. We'll examine each in turn.

1.title: The Enterprise Data Model (EDM)
1.text: The Enterprise Data Model, or EDM, is a holistic, enterprise-level, implementation-independent conceptual or logical data model. Let's unpack that. Holistic and enterprise-level means it spans the whole organization, giving a common, consistent view of data. Implementation-independent means it's not tied to any particular database or technology — and that phrase is testable, so remember it. The EDM captures the key enterprise entities, their relationships, the critical business rules, and some critical attributes. Crucially, it's the foundation for all data-related projects — any project-level model must be based on it. And it's built incrementally and iteratively, in layers, with stakeholders reviewing it to reach consensus. The phrase to lock in: implementation-independent, which is the same idea as technology-agnostic.

1.title: EDM — The 4 Levels of Abstraction
1.text: The Enterprise Data Model is structured across four levels of abstraction, from broadest to most detailed — the widening tiers on screen — and the exam sometimes tests the scales involved. At the top, the Conceptual model is a single diagram of the enterprise's subject areas — typically twelve to twenty significant subject areas with their relationships. Next, each Subject Area model drills into one area, often containing fifty or more significant entities. Then the Logical model adds detail — attributes and the less-significant entities — giving partially attributed views. And finally, the Application or Project models are the logical and physical models scoped to a specific application or project. Two numbers worth remembering: twelve to twenty subject areas at the conceptual level, and fifty-plus entities within a single subject area.

1.title: EDM Linkages & Building Approaches
1.text: Two more concepts about the Enterprise Data Model. First, linkages. Vertical linkages map models between the levels — a physical table maps up to a logical entity, up to a subject-area entity, and so on — which creates model lineage. Horizontal linkages show entities that appear in multiple models at the same level, connecting different subject areas. Second, building approaches. Top-down means you define the subject areas first, then populate them. Bottom-up means you derive the subject-area structure from existing data models. And the combined approach — which the DMBOK recommends — starts bottom-up with your existing models, then completes the picture by delegating subject-area modeling to individual projects. So if asked the recommended approach, the answer is combined.

1.title: Subject Area Discriminators
1.text: How do you decide what goes into each subject area? The DMBOK offers several discriminator principles. You could divide by systems portfolios and funding, by data governance ownership, by top-level business processes or value chains, or by business capabilities. But there's one the DMBOK singles out as the most effective for Data Architecture work: normalization rules. The normalization process establishes the major entities that carry and constitute each subject area, making it the strongest basis for drawing those boundaries. So if a question asks for the most effective subject-area discriminator, the answer is normalization rules.

1.title: Data Flow Design
1.text: Now the second half of Enterprise Data Architecture: data flow design. A data flow is a type of data lineage documentation — it shows how data moves through business processes and systems: where it originates, where it's stored and used, and how it's transformed along the way. Data flows map data to applications, to data stores, to network segments — which is useful for security mapping — to business roles using the CRUD model of create, read, update, delete, and to physical locations. You can document them at the subject-area, entity, or attribute level, and you can represent them as two-dimensional matrices or as data flow diagrams. A nice historical detail the exam sometimes uses: the matrix practice originated with IBM's Business Systems Planning method and was later popularized by James Martin through Information Systems Planning in the 1980s.

1.title: Activities — Establishing the DA Practice (5 Work Streams)
1.text: Let's talk about how you actually stand up a Data Architecture practice. The DMBOK describes five work streams. Strategy: selecting your frameworks, stating your approaches, and developing the roadmap. Acceptance and culture: informing and motivating the behavioral changes that architecture requires. Organization: assigning the accountabilities and responsibilities. Working methods: defining the best practices to use within development projects, in coordination with enterprise architecture. And results: actually producing the Data Architecture artifacts within the overall roadmap. Five work streams — Strategy, Acceptance and Culture, Organization, Working Methods, and Results. Notice that two of the five — acceptance and culture, and organization — are about people and change, not just technical output.

1.title: The Data Architecture Roadmap
1.text: The roadmap is a key deliverable, and it has a few testable specifics. It describes the architecture's three-to-five-year development path — how the target architecture will actually become reality. It's guided by a data management maturity assessment, which we'll cover in a later chapter, and it must be integrated into the overall enterprise architecture roadmap. Now, here's an interesting sequencing rule: a business-data-driven roadmap starts with the most independent business capabilities — the ones with the least dependency on others — and works toward the most dependent. And the most independent capabilities are typically the Master Data areas, like Product Management and Customer Management. So two facts to remember: the roadmap horizon is three to five years, and you start with Master Data because it's the most independent.

1.title: Managing Enterprise Requirements within Projects
1.text: Architecture has to coexist with real delivery projects, whatever methodology those projects use. At the end of a project, architects determine whether the enterprise-wide entities conform to the agreed standards, what should be folded into the overall Enterprise Data Architecture, and whether definitions need generalizing for future trends. And the implementation approach adapts to the method. In Waterfall, you work through sequential phases with tollgates, making sure the enterprise perspective is included. In Incremental delivery, you use mini-waterfalls with comprehensive data design in the early iterations. And in Agile or iterative delivery, you work in sprints, delivering data model specifications for how data is captured, stored, and distributed. The constant across all three: the enterprise data perspective must be preserved no matter the methodology.

1.title: Tools & Techniques
1.text: Quickly, the tools and techniques. On tools: data modeling tools manage the Enterprise Data Model and track lineage between models; asset management software inventories your systems and collects metadata about them; and graphical design applications help you create the diagrams, data flows, and value chains. On techniques, there are two worth knowing. Lifecycle projections classify technology products by their status — we'll see the eight statuses on the next slide. And diagramming clarity is a set of six characteristics that keep architectural diagrams readable: a clear consistent legend, a match between diagram objects and the legend, consistent line direction, consistent handling of line crossings, meaningful object attributes, and linear symmetry. Clear diagrams communicate; messy ones mislead.

1.title: Technique — Lifecycle Projections (8 Statuses)
1.text: The lifecycle projection technique assigns one of eight statuses to each technology product, which helps you plan what to adopt and what to retire. Current means supported and in use now. Deployment means it'll be deployed within the next one to two years. Strategic means it's expected to be available in two or more years. Retirement means it's being retired within a year. Preferred means it's the go-to choice for most applications. Containment means its use is limited to certain applications. Emerging means it's being researched or piloted. And Reviewed means it's been evaluated but doesn't currently fall into any other status. The two timeframes worth memorizing are Deployment at one-to-two years and Strategic at two-plus years.

1.title: Implementation Guidelines & 7 Risks
1.text: When implementing Data Architecture, there are four components: organizing the teams and forums, producing the initial artifacts like the enterprise data model and roadmaps, embedding an architectural way of working into projects, and building awareness of the value of architecture across the organization. The traditional starting point is the Master Data areas, where the need for improvement is greatest, then expanding to transactional data. Now, the DMBOK lists seven implementation risks, and you should at least recognize them: lack of management support, no proven track record, an apprehensive sponsor, counter-productive executive decisions, culture shock, an inexperienced project leader, and the dominance of a one-dimensional view — like the owners of a single ERP system trying to dictate the entire enterprise architecture. The single most significant risk is the first one: lack of management support.

1.title: Cultural Factors & DA Governance
1.text: Adopting Data Architecture is as much cultural as technical. The DMBOK names six cultural factors, and the themes are: having an architecture-friendly culture, recognizing data as a business asset rather than just an IT concern, being able to let go of a local perspective in favor of an enterprise one, integrating architectural deliverables into project methods, accepting formal data governance, and being able to look at the enterprise holistically. On the governance side, there are four Data Architecture governance activities: overseeing projects for compliance, managing the designs lifecycle and tools — where the Enterprise Data Architecture acts like a zoning plan for long-term integration — defining standards, and creating data-related artifacts. And the ideal arrangement is to assign both a Data Architect and a Data Steward to each subject area, pairing design expertise with stewardship accountability.

1.title: Metrics — 3 Categories
1.text: Data Architecture is measured across three categories. The architecture standard compliance rate measures how closely projects comply with the established architectures, tracking exceptions as obstacles to adoption. Implementation trends look at use, reuse, replace, and retire measurements — the proportion of new versus reused artifacts — plus project execution efficiency, like lead times and resource costs. And business value measurements capture things like business agility improvements, whether business cases are fulfilled, operational quality gains, and broader environmental improvements such as better client retention or fewer regulatory remarks. Three categories: compliance rate, implementation trends, and business value.

1.title: Key Numbers & Quick Facts (Cheat Sheet)
1.text: Let's consolidate the numbers for this chapter. Data Architecture has three goals. There are four EA domains — Business, Data, Applications, Technology. The Zachman Framework is a six-by-six matrix developed by Zachman in the 1980s, with columns what, how, where, who, when, why, and rows planner, owner, designer, builder, implementer, and participant — and remember the participant row has no models. Enterprise Data Architecture has two outputs: the Enterprise Data Model and the Data Flow Design. The EDM has four levels, with twelve to twenty subject areas at the conceptual level. The best subject-area discriminator is normalization rules. The roadmap horizon is three to five years. There are five work streams, seven risks, and eight lifecycle statuses. Drill these until they're automatic.

1.title: Common Exam Traps
1.text: Here are the traps for this chapter. First, the big one: Zachman does not tell you how to build models — it shows what models should exist. Any answer saying Zachman is a methodology is wrong. Second, Data Architecture is not standalone — it's one of four EA domains. Third, the Enterprise Data Model is implementation-independent, or technology-agnostic; don't pick answers that tie it to a specific database or platform. Fourth, the roadmap starts with the most independent capabilities, typically Master Data — not the most complex or dependent ones. And fifth, remember the Zachman User, or Participant, row has no models; it's the live, running enterprise. Watch for the signature phrases "master blueprints" and "implementation-independent" — they point you to the right answers.

1.title: Module Summary
1.text: Let's wrap up. Data Architecture designs and maintains the master blueprints that align data with business strategy — it's the bridge between business and technology. It's one of four enterprise architecture domains, and the Zachman Framework is a six-by-six ontology that tells you what, not how. Enterprise Data Architecture has two parts: the Enterprise Data Model, with its four levels, and the Data Flow Design — and the EDM is implementation-independent. The roadmap spans three to five years and starts with Master Data. And keep in mind the seven implementation risks — especially lack of management support — and the three metric categories. That's Chapter 4.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Let's test what you've learned with five questions. Question one: in the Zachman Framework, which artifact addresses "What" from the system designer's perspective, Row 3? The answer is D — the entity-relationship diagram defining the logical data model. Row 3 is the Architect or Designer, and the "What" column there is the logical data model. The physical schema would be Row 4, and a data flow diagram answers "How," not "What."

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two: which notations document data architecture at the conceptual and logical levels? The answer is C — entity-relationship diagrams and data flow diagrams. The other options describe network, deployment, or business-process notations.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three: which statement exemplifies a technology-agnostic principle? The answer is D — managing data to support business needs independent of any specific platform. The Enterprise Data Model is implementation-independent. Tying it to a relational database, an ERP, or a cloud vendor is the opposite.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four: how does an ontology differ from a taxonomy? The answer is D — a taxonomy is a strict hierarchy, while an ontology captures richer, multi-relational concepts and the logical rules among them. Recall that Zachman itself is described as an ontology. And

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: question five: the primary output of a current-versus-target architecture assessment? The answer is B — a gap analysis with prioritized initiatives, which drives the transformation roadmap. A full physical model, a task-level plan, or a vendor scorecard are not the guiding output. That completes Module 4. Next up is one of the big ones — Module 5, Data Modeling and Design, an eleven-percent chapter. I'll see you there.
